items.title: 66100_Bud Freeman oral history interview
items.q: Art Hodes called me from Chicago ... And he asked me if I'd come out.

ctx.x: The point is, it happened to you and if it had been one of those that happened so fast that you didn't know anything about it, but you had a few seconds.

Well, I was very lucky. I had no ill effects from it. The first show I did, I didn't do anything for seven months, and Art Hodes called me from Chicago -- he had that wonderful show, I think it was called Blues Alley. And he asked me if I'd come out. And the doctor said now you might feel some pain when you start to play again, because the expansion and all, but there was nothing. No pain, it was marvelous and I played that first thing and that started me all over again.
You mean you actually hadn't blown, you hadn't played at all.

items.title: 67559_Art Hodes oral history interview
items.q: It was Freeman and the whole band. Krupa -- I know Krupa and Freeman were in that band together. We played the floor show, we played everything.

ctx.x: And you had worked together, made the record. Was there a place called the Cellar that you worked at during that period?

Yes, My Cellar was a place and the Three Deuces was a place. And Winnie and I broke up after the El Dorado Club. We had gone out to the El Dorado Club, we were still talking, but I had met a New Orleans kid by the name of Bill Kennedy, who was a fighter. He'd been a great fighter. Fought for the championship and all that. Lost, but he'd been a great lightweight fighter.

And he loved this music. There was a fascination between us. We liked each other. And he didn't like what was happening to him. He kept telling me that Winnie was just taking me. I was paying for my musical education, is what he was saying. And of course, in the El Dorado Club after that, we were still together, but this thing was going on underneath.
